cond_about.swarm: ten drones wrapped round each goal building, a feed per hull drone on the ring of screens
cond_about.single: one drone, the trials' forward camera on one screen
cond_about.sphere: one drone flown the single drone's way, its 360 camera on a sphere round the pilot as a 2K stream

answer: The swarm beats one drone: it takes 0.75× the time, all of the gain at the goal. internal_4's pilots measured 0.86×.
Against a 360 drone shown at full resolution, the swarm only ties (1.00×). Seeing every way from one place is as good as ten spread-out views, provided the picture is sharp.

The swarm's large lead over the 360 drone (0.61×) comes from resolution, not from the viewpoints. The main study showed that drone through a 2K live stream, about a third of a feed screen's pixels per degree. Its pilot could not make out a hat until close to it, and it finished the task in 2% of sessions.
reading_short: So the 360 comparison measures the display: the swarm beats a blurry 360 view and ties a sharp one. Nobody has flown the 2K stream, so the human trial will be decided by how sharp a real 360 drone's live view is.
reading: Both verdicts are the swarm's, on either credit. Press-credited, swarm ÷ 360 drone 0.61 (0.59–0.64) and swarm ÷ one drone 0.75 (0.71–0.79); first sight, 0.56 (0.54–0.59) and 0.81 (0.76–0.86). The 360 drone finished within the 900 s cap in only 2% of sessions (the swarm 86%, one drone 63%), so its restricted mean sits against the cap and the ratio against it is, if anything, kind to it.

The swarm's lead is at the goal and nowhere else. Per goal at the goal the swarm takes 37 s, one drone 83 s, the 360 drone 198 s. Between goals the swarm is level with the 360 drone (0.97×) and slower than one drone (1.13×): ten drones fly no faster than one, and they notice a crowd about as far off (137 m median against 128 m).

It is the spread of the viewpoints, not the number of feeds. At a goal the wrapped swarm recognises at 2.80 hats a minute. The same ten feeds moved to the formation's centre manage 0.09 (31× fewer; partly because the centre of a wrapped swarm is inside the building), and a 360 camera on its most central drone, at the swarm's height, 0.016 (173× fewer). Round a building the drones stand on every side of it, close to whoever is walking there; one camera, however wide, stands on one side.

Why the stream does so badly. A 2K equirectangular frame spreads 2048 pixels over 360°, 5.7 per degree against the feed screens' 17.7 reaching the eye, so a hat counts 3.1× as far away. The hazard is steep (k 5.3), so a hat 20 m off, an easy recognition on a feed, becomes one at 62 m, almost none. The 360 drone's recognitions came at a median 10.7 m against one drone's 22.3 m: it had to fly up to each hat. On its own flights a forward camera would have recognised 7× as often; on one drone's flights a 2K 360 camera would have recognised 0.13× as often as the forward camera did.

The resolution is the whole question about the 360 drone. Every sensitivity but the display leaves swarm ÷ 360 drone between 0.60 and 0.75 (the hat's distance ×0.75 or ×1.33, the crowd's at 200 or 400 m, the walk without exploring, the 360 drone flown SIMI's way or at SIMI's altitudes, the swarm circling instead of wrapping). Halve the stream's cost and leave the crowd unscaled: 0.75 (0.69–0.81), still the swarm's. Show the cube SIMI flew: 1.00 (0.90–1.10), equivalent within 10%, with the 360 drone then 0.79× one drone's time, a better camera than the forward one. Scaling the hat but not the crowd changes little (0.66), so it is recognising the hat, not noticing the crowd, that the stream loses.

Against one drone the answer does not move. Swarm ÷ one drone stays between 0.73 and 0.82 across the sensitivities, and in the three held-out cities (per city, never pooled) it is 0.78, 0.82, 0.73, with swarm ÷ 360 drone 0.64, 0.64, 0.61; every interval's upper end is at most 0.89.

The model is slower than the people, between goals. internal_4's geometric-mean task times were 436 s with the swarm and 507 s with one drone; the model's restricted means are 550 s and 731 s. The calibration gate (passed 5 of 8, press-credited) placed the gap between goals: the scripted pilot wanders where people head for the next crowd. The ratios are what the model is trusted for, and they agree: swarm ÷ one drone 0.75 against the people's 0.86, at the goal 0.45 against 0.50 (0.32–0.78).

The swarm pays for it in drones. It lost 199 drones and touched buildings 391 times over 300 sessions (0.66 drones a session), no session ending under four drones. Unity's headless bench agreed with the replica on route time, wrapping and losses (the spot check).

What the human retest should expect, and fly. Swarm ÷ one drone near 0.75: with two runs per condition and internal_4's run-to-run spread (SD 0.30 in log time), about 18 pilots for 80% power. Swarm ÷ the 360 stream near 0.61: about 8 pilots. But the stream's cost is this study's one unmeasured input, and at the cube's resolution the answer flips to a tie, which no feasible number of pilots could separate from 10%. So the retest should fly the 360 drone on the stream, as the sphere now shows it, and the first thing to read from it is the distance at which pilots name a hat through the stream: about 8 m at half-rate if this model is right, 26 m if the stream costs nothing.
intro: 300 sessions in the trial city, each flown in all three conditions with the same three goals, hats and walkers and the same random thresholds, so every comparison is paired. Task time is the restricted mean to the 900 s cap (a session not done counts to the cap; a swarm under four drones to where it stopped), with 95% bootstrap intervals over sessions. The verdict rule was written before the run (rule.json): an interval wholly below 0.9 means the swarm is at least 10% faster, wholly above 1/0.9 the other condition is, wholly inside the green band equivalent within 10%. Recognition is credited at the press (the credit the calibration gate passed); first-sight credit is shown hollow.

probe.text: The probe searches every goal for exactly 120 s whatever is recognised, so every view of the same flight is scored over the same window (100 sessions, 798 goals). On the swarm's own flights, wrapped round the goal building, its spread-out feeds recognise 173 (121–265)× the hats of a 360 camera with the 2K stream on its most central drone at the swarm's height (262 (193–373)× at the 360 drone's 9.9 m), and 31 (24–41)× the same ten feeds moved to its centre. On the 360 drone's flights the stream recognises 0.14 (0.12–0.17)× what a forward camera would; on one drone's flights a 360 stream would recognise 0.13 (0.11–0.15)× its forward camera.

stream.text: internal_4's only 360 flights (SIMI's) showed the cube itself, about 22 pixels per degree reaching the eye, more than a feed screen's 17.8. Since 2026-11-18 the sphere shows what a real 360 drone's live link carries, the Antigravity A1's 2K view: 5.7 pixels per degree, so a hat at d metres covers as many pixels as one 3.1 d metres away on a feed. Recognising a 21 cm hat is a matter of pixels across it, so the stream puts the 360 drone's hats 3.1 times further away, its half-rate distance at 8 m instead of 26 m, and a crowd's at 90 m instead of 282 m. No one has flown the stream yet, so this part is a model, not a measurement: the ratios below put it beside the cube SIMI flew and beside a stream that costs half as much.
stream.caption: Swarm ÷ 360 drone and 360 drone ÷ one drone, task times, with the 360 drone's display as flown in the main study (the 2K stream), as SIMI flew it (the cube) and with the stream's cost halved in log (the hat's distance × √3.1, the crowd's not scaled): the optimistic bound.

changes: YEGO's four runs joined internal_4 (two swarm, two one-drone, ScenicPatchCityWorld, 2026-11-18): 54 correct presses instead of 41, 4 pilots instead of 3. On the proposal's basis the hat's half-rate distance went 31 → 25 m: YEGO flew one drone at about 2 m and the swarm low, and recognised up close.
A hat counts anywhere in the frame, as the recorder has scored since 2026-11-18, not only in its central 80%: the four presses the old basis could not explain are explained (d50 25 m).

The 360 drone shows the 2K live stream (Sphere360Display.streamWidth 2048 since 2026-11-18), about a third of the pixels per degree a feed screen delivers, where SIMI flew the cube. Distances are now fitted in pixel-equivalent metres (d50 26 m at the feeds), and the 360 drone's hats and crowds count 3.1× further away. No human has flown the stream yet: this is a model of it, not a measurement.
The crowd's noticing curve has a fixed shape (k 8): with YEGO's legs its steepness is not identified. Walkers are drawn to 500 m (the scenes' sleep distance since 2026-11-18, 350 before).

Altitudes and gimbal pitches are the median over pilots of each pilot's median, so YEGO's 2 m single-drone flying counts once: one drone 6.6 m at a goal (was 7.0), the swarm 7.2 m (10.4), the sphere as SIMI flew 9.9 m (14.3).
The verdict is read on press-credited recognition, the credit the calibration gate passes with the new fits (first sight was the better one before, and is now faster than the people at the goal).

The swarm wraps every goal building and the 360 drone flies the single drone's searches at its altitudes (the experimenter's two calls in review), so the 360 drone and one drone differ only in the camera.

rec.text: For every goal, each 0.1 s the hat was on a shown screen inside the head's view with a clear line is exposure, and the press (credited 1 s before it) an event. The hazard by distance is fitted as λ(d) = λ0 / (1 + (d/d50)^k): λ0 0.57/s, half that at 26 m (95% 19–32), a tenth at 40 m (k 5.3), over 54 presses. Credited at the start of the final sighting instead: λ0 1.92/s, d50 22 m. The proposal's fit, before YEGO, on the central 80%: λ0 0.49, d50 31 m.
rec.caption: Dots: presses per second of exposure in distance bins, with 95% intervals; lines: the fits.
rec.note: Each pilot's own fit; YEGO, who flew one drone at about 2 m, recognised quickly but only up close. Distances are pixel-equivalent at the trials' feeds (below); for the feed conditions they are metres.

res.text: Distances are fitted in pixel-equivalent metres: a hat d metres away on a display that delivers r pixels per world degree counts as d × r_feed / r metres, r_feed being the trials' feeds on their 60° screens. What reaches the eye is the lesser of what the image holds and what the headset (about 22 px/deg) shows of it.

terms: Ten drones at d_ref 2.0 under BlockShapedPatchCityWorld's law; the hull drones' feeds on a ring of 60° screens round the pilot; at a goal it flies to the centre building and holds there so the formation wraps it.
One drone with the trials' forward camera on one screen, searching a goal by working round the ring buildings, orbiting some with the camera turned in and passing others, stopping to look round.
The same drone and the same searches, its 360 camera shown on a sphere round the pilot as the Antigravity A1's 2K live stream; the pilot's head picks where to look.
A building with a ring of buildings across the streets round it, 16 pedestrians walking round each ring building, one wearing the hat; three goals per session, drawn as BlockGoals draws them at Play.
A goal's time is split at its zone (the patch grown by 15 m): from the previous press to the zone is between goals, from the zone to the press at the goal.
From the start line to the press on the third hat; the restricted mean to 900 s over sessions.
One goal draw (goals, hats, walkers, the random thresholds) flown in every condition: the unit of every interval.
Hat recognitions per second while the hat is on a screen in the head's view with a clear line, as a function of distance: λ0 / (1 + (d/d50)^k), fitted to internal_4.
A recognition credited at the press (1 s before it), or at the start of the final continuous sighting before it (pilots sometimes closed in to check). The two bound the truth.
The same for a goal's crowd: noticed per second while its walkers are expected on the head's screens.
A distance scaled by the trials' feeds' pixels per degree over the display's: the 2K stream counts 3.1× further, SIMI's cube 0.81×.
Every goal searched for exactly 120 s whatever is recognised, so different views of the same flight are scored over the same window.
The replica flown from Unity's recorded start along the same route, for the spot check.
